stories.headline: Shoe Station Group Dramatically Halts Store Conversions, to Revert Most Locations to Original Banner
stories.claim: Shoe Station Group halts store conversions and will return most of its 131 rebannered stores to their original banners.
stories.summary: Shoe Station Group, the US footwear retailer formerly known as Shoe Carnival, is reversing much of its store rebannering strategy. On its third-quarter call on Tuesday, interim chief executive Cliff Sifford said 104 of the 131 rebannered stores are still under review, with at least 75 per cent expected to revert to the Shoe Carnival name, while 27 Shoe Station at Rogan's stores will return to Rogan's. The company said the upgraded product and higher prices had alienated the Shoe Carnival customer. Returning stores will cost $2 million to $3 million, plus about $4 million in fourth-quarter expenses, mostly falling in fiscal 2027. The move follows a sharp earnings miss and a fall in the share price, and it puts the turnaround strategy under scrutiny.
key_points: Shoe Station Group will return most of its 131 rebannered stores to the Shoe Carnival or Rogan's names, with 27 Shoe Station at Rogan's locations going back to Rogan's.
Management estimates at least 75 per cent of the 104 stores still under review will revert to Shoe Carnival, with a final number due in the next few weeks.
In-store changes start in early December for the holiday season, with formal banner changes expected in the first quarter of fiscal 2027 because of permits and signage.
The company expects about $4 million of fourth-quarter expenses plus $2 million to $3 million of banner costs, mainly in fiscal 2027, without changing fiscal 2026 guidance.

Interim CEO Cliff Sifford said the upgraded product and higher prices had alienated Shoe Carnival's core customer, and that future growth will come from higher-income areas under the Shoe Carnival banner.
stories.market_take: A strategic U-turn and extra costs weigh on the shares, which already fell sharply after the earnings miss.

stories.headline: Marc Jacobs Sales Hit $509M in Its Last Year Under LVMH
stories.claim: Marc Jacobs generated $509m revenue in 2025, its last year under LVMH, according to a new SEC filing.
stories.summary: A recent SEC filing shows Marc Jacobs made $509 million in revenue in 2025, its last year under LVMH, and an operating profit of $106.8 million. After interest of $35.1 million, mostly on $525 million of loans owed to LVMH, comprehensive income was $71.1 million. G-III Apparel Group and WHP Global bought the brand in September for nearly $900 million combined, and more than half of that went to repay the loans. G-III chief executive Morris Goldfarb says the brand will focus on handbags, small leather goods and accessories, expand licensing and bring back the Marc by Marc Jacobs sub-label. He has set a long-term target of $1 billion in annual revenue.

G-III paid $468.8 million at closing for the operating company and half the brand, with WHP contributing about $425 million for its half.

stories.market_take: The filing gives investors a clearer view of the brand's economics under G-III and WHP, though G-III is a small listing with limited direct exposure.

stories.headline: ‘Costly’ Air Freight is Bangladesh Apparel Exporters’ Fallback Option as Orders Slip
stories.claim: Bangladesh garment exporters are paying costly air freight to ship late orders as labour unrest disrupts production and buyers shift orders.
stories.summary: Bangladeshi garment factories are paying steep premiums to fly late orders out of the country, as wage unrest that began in October has pushed foreign buyers to look elsewhere. The BGMEA says factories have already lost an estimated $428 million from production disruptions, a figure it says excludes extra air freight costs, discounts and cancellations. Buyers have moved 59 million pieces of confirmed orders, worth $254 million, to other countries between 1 and 18 November. Air cargo data from WorldACD shows Bangladesh-to-US tonnage up 38 to 44 percent year on year in October and November, while Dhaka's airport remains strained by a cargo station fire last October. The wage board is weighing a demand to lift the minimum wage from 12,500 taka (about $100) to 30,000 taka (about $240), with factory owners eyeing roughly 15 percent. The row matters for global apparel supply chains and for brands sourcing from Bangladesh.
key_points: BGMEA says factories have lost an estimated $428 million, excluding extra air freight, discounts and cancellations.
Buyers have shifted 59 million pieces of confirmed orders worth $254 million to other countries from 1 to 18 November.
US-bound air freight from Bangladesh rose 44% year on year in mid-October and 38% in mid-November, according to WorldACD.
Workers want the monthly minimum wage raised from 12,500 taka to 30,000 taka; factory owners are reportedly eyeing about a 15% rise.
Dhaka airport's import backlog reached 400 to 500 metric tons, against over 100 before a fire last October, constraining air capacity.
The government formed a minimum wage board on 1 November; talks were ongoing and about 481 factories were halted on one day.
stories.market_take: Limited direct listed exposure; higher costs and delays could hit apparel importers and brands sourcing from Bangladesh.

stories.headline: Saks Fifth Avenue Unveils Holiday Windows Amid Protests Over Alleged Employee Treatment
stories.claim: Saks Fifth Avenue unveiled its holiday windows and light show in New York as protesters over alleged staff mistreatment gathered outside.
stories.summary: Saks Fifth Avenue staged its annual holiday light show and window unveiling on its Manhattan flagship, closing Fifth Avenue between 49th and 50th Streets, despite about 90 protesters outside. The protest was organised by Jeff Vinokur, a former Generation Genius founder, on behalf of his mother, a former sales associate who says she was harassed by a customer in June. The windows, themed around two New York pigeons, took five to six months to produce and about 3,300 hours of work. The show runs until 3 January, with a Make-A-Wish fundraiser and a Bread Financial sponsorship. The event comes as the parent group, Exemplar Luxury, emerged from bankruptcy in June with new owners and fewer stores.

stories.headline: Victoria’s Secret’s Switch at the Top, Chair Donna James Steps Down
stories.claim: Victoria's Secret chair Donna James is stepping down after the next annual meeting, with Edgewell CEO Rod Little to take over.
stories.summary: Donna James, who led Victoria's Secret & Co. since its 2021 spin-off from L Brands, is stepping down as chair after the next annual meeting. Rod Little, chief executive of Edgewell Personal Care and a board member since 2023, will become chair. The handover comes as the company's turnaround under CEO Hillary Super gathers pace: first-half sales rose 12.7% to $3.2 billion and the shares have risen. James had faced criticism from activist Brett Blundy's BBRC International, which argued the board had waited too long to replace the previous CEO and that excessive tenure hurt governance. Her re-election to the board nonetheless passed with more than 99% of votes at the annual meeting.

Rod Little has led Edgewell Personal Care since 2019 and spent 17 years at Procter & Gamble.

stories.headline: Kohl’s Returns to Growth in Q3, Raises Outlook
stories.claim: Kohl's returned to sales growth in its third quarter and raised its full-year outlook, sending shares up 19.5%.
stories.summary: Kohl's shares jumped 19.5% to $25.33 after the retailer reported its first sales growth in more than five years and lifted its full-year guidance. Third-quarter net sales rose 1.3% to $3.45 billion, with comparable sales up 1.2%. Net income was $254 million, or $2.15 a diluted share, helped by tax benefits, a real estate gain and tariff refunds; a year earlier it earned $8 million. Full-year net sales are now expected to be flat to up 0.5%, up from a previous decline of 1.5% to flat, with diluted EPS guided to $4.30 to $4.50. CEO Michael Bender credited a turnaround built on clearer value messaging and stronger proprietary brands, though he flagged softness in cold-weather categories.

Net income of $254 million was boosted by one-off items including tax benefits, a real estate gain and tariff refunds.
Full-year sales guidance was lifted to flat to up 0.5%, with diluted EPS guided to $4.30 to $4.50.
Gross margin rose 1.45 percentage points and inventory fell 1% to $3.9 billion, reducing clearance risk.
stories.market_take: Strong share price reaction to a guidance raise; the stock has a turnaround narrative but is a small-cap retailer.

stories.headline: Abercrombie & Fitch Powers Through Another Strong Quarter, Raises Outlook
stories.claim: Abercrombie & Fitch shares soared nearly 20% after a strong third quarter and a raised 2026 outlook.
stories.summary: Abercrombie & Fitch shares jumped 19.7% on Thursday after the retailer reported a strong third quarter and raised its outlook for 2026. Net sales rose 11% to $1.4 billion, with comparable sales up 6%, and operating income reached $223 million against $155 million a year earlier. Diluted EPS rose to $3.82 from $2.36. The company now expects 6% sales growth for the year, up from 5%, and EPS of $13.70 to $13.90, up from $13.10 to $13.60. CEO Fran Horowitz credited tight inventory control, fewer promotions and growth across brands, and said the Hollister home category test with Target was being evaluated. The 16th consecutive quarter of growth gives the company a strong run into the holiday season.

stories.headline: US Treasury financial crime watchdog hit by suspected cyber attack
stories.claim: US Treasury's FinCEN took systems offline after a cyber incident involving unauthorised access to a limited set of systems.
stories.summary: The US Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has taken some of its systems offline after detecting unauthorised access to a limited subset of its systems. An agency official said the move was precautionary and that filers unable to submit reports were given temporary relief. The Treasury is working with the FBI, CISA and third-party forensic examiners to establish the scope and impact. A person familiar with the matter said there is no evidence so far of a breach of Bank Secrecy Act or beneficial ownership databases. The incident comes amid a run of technology failures in the US this month, including a nationwide air travel halt and a Microsoft email outage.

stories.headline: ESA's Hera probe finds DART left a stadium-sized crater on asteroid Dimorphos
stories.claim: ESA's Hera probe shows NASA's DART impact left a stadium-sized crater on asteroid Dimorphos, which now tumbles in orbit.
stories.summary: The European Space Agency's Hera probe has sent back its first close views of the aftermath of NASA's 2022 DART impact on Dimorphos, the moon of asteroid Didymos. The images show a crater roughly the size of a sports stadium, stretching across nearly the asteroid's entire 151-metre width, and the body now tumbles in its orbit instead of keeping one face toward Didymos. Hera also identified more than 100 boulders in a debris field larger than the team expected. Scientists had predicted a crater of about 20 metres, and the orbit was shortened by 33 minutes and 15 seconds, far beyond NASA's 73-second target, suggesting debris amplified the push. Hera will move from 25-30 km to about 13 km for higher-resolution imaging, and two CubeSats, Juventas and Milani, are due to deploy in early 2027 to attempt landings and collect data. The mission is slated to last six months. The results will refine models of how effectively a spacecraft can deflect a dangerous asteroid.
key_points: Hera has revealed a crater roughly the size of a sports stadium on Dimorphos, stretching across the asteroid's full 151-metre width.
Dimorphos now tumbles in its orbit rather than keeping one face toward its partner Didymos.
More than 100 boulders have been identified in a debris field larger than expected.
The orbit was shortened by 33 minutes 15 seconds, far beyond NASA's 73-second target, indicating debris amplified the push.
Hera will move closer to about 13 km, and the CubeSats Juventas and Milani are due to deploy in early 2027.
The findings will help planetary defence planning for future asteroid deflection missions.

stories.claim: US is reportedly preparing to unveil new Section 301 tariffs on at least 14 trading partners, including China, the EU and Japan.

stories.headline: H&M: Advancing an Already Mature Business in North America
stories.claim: H&M details North American growth plans, including Puerto Rico expansion and wider rollout of its Move activewear line.
stories.summary: H&M, the Swedish fast-fashion group, says its 26-year-old North American business is mature but still has room to grow, with 478 stores in the US and 89 in Canada. The company opened its third Puerto Rico store in Ponce on 19 November, with a fourth planned at Plaza Las Américas in San Juan for summer 2027, together creating about 65 jobs. Managing director Aneta Pokucinska told WWD that H&M is tailoring ranges to local climates, broadening streetwear and leisure lines, and adding its H&M Move activewear to more than 100 further US stores in December. Over the next year H&M will also donate $100,000 to a Puerto Rican water-resilience nonprofit. The interview shows how the group is trying to grow in a mature market through localisation rather than simply adding stores.

A third Puerto Rico store opened in Ponce on 19 November, a 21,257 sq ft site selling women's, men's and kids' clothing.

H&M will donate $100,000 over the next year to Foundation for Puerto Rico, a nonprofit backing a water-resilience initiative amid drought.
H&M Move activewear expanded to more than 250 extra US stores this year and is set to reach more than 100 additional stores in December.

stories.headline: Supermodel Veruschka, 1960s icon, dies at 87
stories.claim: German-born supermodel Veruschka, a 1960s icon, has died at 87, Bild confirmed on 25 November.
stories.summary: Veruschka, the German-born supermodel known for her shape-shifting presence and body art, has died aged 87, according to Bild, which confirmed the news on 25 November. She died at home surrounded by friends and family. Born Vera von Lehndorff-Steinort in Königsberg in 1939, she was discovered in Florence in 1959 and became one of the first supermodels, appearing on 13 American Vogue covers and on the British Vogue cover in February 1969. She worked with Richard Avedon, Irving Penn, Horst P. Horst and David Bailey, and played a version of herself in Michelangelo Antonioni's 1966 film Blow-Up. Later she turned to art photography with Holger Trülzsch and made occasional runway returns, including for Chanel in 1994 and Giles Deacon in 2011. Her childhood was marked by the Nazi regime, after her father was executed following the 1944 plot against Hitler.

stories.headline: Too Much, Too Little: Bangladesh’s Wage Hike Pleases No One
stories.claim: Bangladesh's wage board raised the garment minimum wage 36% to 17,000 taka, a hike unions and brands both criticise.
stories.summary: Bangladesh has lifted the monthly minimum wage for garment workers by 36 percent, to 17,000 taka (about $136), after a wage board vote of 4-2. It is the smallest percentage rise for the sector in four decades, and it came after weeks of street protests that had shut 87 factories in Ashulia, Savar and Gazipur. Workers had demanded 30,000 to 32,000 taka, while factory owners had initially offered 15,000 taka. Union leaders called the outcome 'not respectful', while employers argue that direct labour costs of about 42 cents per garment, above rivals in Vietnam and India, leave margins too thin. Brands are being urged to pay higher prices, and rights groups warn that factories could push unpaid overtime to offset the rise. The outcome matters for the world's second-largest apparel exporter and for the buyers sourcing from it.

About 87 factories in Ashulia, Savar and Gazipur remained closed as of Wednesday amid the protests.

Rights groups warn that factories may force unpaid overtime and unrealistic targets, and urge brands to share the cost through higher purchase prices.
The next wage revision comes after three years, sooner than the previous five-year cycle.
stories.market_take: Little direct market impact; a modest cost pressure for apparel exporters and the brands that source from Bangladesh.

Arnault's net worth is estimated at about $130 billion by Bloomberg, and five of his children work inside LVMH.

Fielkow previously ran Tetra Pak units in Vietnam, the US and Canada. The changes are routine leadership moves in the apparel industry, though the Lululemon hire is part of a wider reshuffle as the company tries to reset its image and performance.

stories.headline: This Riviera mayor wants to bring Javier Milei’s chainsaw politics to France
stories.claim: Cannes mayor David Lisnard, pitching Milei-style spending cuts, surges in French presidential polling and re-elected head of mayors' lobby.
stories.summary: David Lisnard, the right-wing mayor of Cannes, is becoming a surprise force in France's presidential race, polling around 11% in the first round, level with centre-right Édouard Philippe and centre-left Raphaël Glucksmann. He wants to cut €200 billion from public spending, shed 400,000 civil service jobs and shred large parts of labour, environmental and planning law, openly praising Argentina's Javier Milei. On Wednesday he was re-elected president of the Association des maires de France with 72% of the vote, a platform that some mayors say he is using to boost his presidential bid. Rivals call him a 'masked Macronist' or accuse him of plotting a far-right alliance, while he refuses questions on his candidacy. The race is already crowded with Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon leading, so his rise could reshape the centre-right vote.

stories.headline: MoD tells 100,000 reservists: be ready for call-up
stories.claim: UK Ministry of Defence has sent letters to about 100,000 reservists and veterans telling them to prepare for possible call-up.
stories.summary: Britain's Ministry of Defence has written to about 100,000 strategic reservists and recently departed veterans, telling them to be ready for a possible call-up, the first such move since the Cold War. The letters, signed by the chiefs of all three armed services, invite volunteers for training such as Nato's Steadfast Defender exercise next spring and ask recipients to update their contact details and skills. The MoD says the aim is to strengthen preparedness and deterrence and improve data on former personnel, and insists mobilisation is not being suggested. The move follows Russian cruise missiles and a drone entering eastern Poland last week, and comes as Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has warned Britain must be ready for war within 1,000 days. The British Army is currently at its smallest size since the Napoleonic Wars, with about 73,000 active personnel.

Justice Minister Waldemar Żurek estimates compensation payments could exceed €12 million and may grow as judges appointed under the disputed system keep hearing cases. He blamed PiS for the damage and accused President Karol Nawrocki of obstructing repairs, after Nawrocki vetoed a reform bill in February. stories.headline: Japan's data centre boom faces growing revolt from urban residents
stories.claim: Japan's data centre boom is facing rising resident opposition in Tokyo and other urban areas, prompting a government review.
stories.summary: Japan's data centre construction boom is running into growing anger from residents, with about 60% of facilities concentrated in and around Tokyo. In Kashiwa, two 31-metre data centres owned by Hong Kong-based PAG loom over homes and send generator fumes into the air. In Tokyo's Koto ward, residents are fighting a planned 51-metre facility by Singapore-based Empyrion Digital, due for completion in 2029, which would bury 1.2 million litres of heavy oil in a flood-prone, high-earthquake-risk area. Residents have appealed to the Tokyo metropolitan assembly for binding rules on noise, heat and fuel safety. The government is reviewing the industry, and an action plan is due by the end of 2026. Consultancy JLL forecasts Japan's data centre market will reach $33.4 billion by 2030, up from $23.4 billion in 2024.

stories.headline: King tides and storms threaten US coasts; Macy's moves Thanksgiving parade to Saturday
stories.claim: Record king tides cause coastal flooding in California as storms batter both US coasts during Thanksgiving; Macy's moves its parade to Saturday.
stories.summary: Macy's has postponed the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade for the first time in its history, moving it from Thursday 27 November to Saturday 28 November because of forecasts of severe storms in New York, with a step-off at 8.30am. Forecasts for Thursday called for heavy rain, strong gusts and localised flooding, with balloons grounded above 34 mph gusts, while the Saturday forecast is much milder, with a low chance of rain and winds of up to 14 mph. The move is a major logistical challenge for about 11,000 volunteers, 100 inflatable elements and broadcast partners NBC, Peacock and Telemundo. Elsewhere, record-high king tides peaked on Wednesday and Thursday along the California coast, with water levels over 8 feet in some areas. San Diego recorded 8 ft 11 in, potentially a record, while Los Angeles hit about 8.19 ft, a city record. A developing nor'easter threatens heavy rain, strong winds and coastal flooding on the US East Coast, with up to six inches of rain possible in coastal North Carolina. The National Weather Service links the high tides to the strongest El Niño on record. The AAA expects 81.5 million Americans to travel at least 50 miles over the holiday, so disruption could affect millions.

Its shares closed down 85% on Wednesday, hitting an all-time low and wiping out most of the market value it had left this year. The squeeze is hitting Europe's weaker carriers hard, with airBaltic in Chapter 11 and EasyJet's sale to Apollo Global Management in train.

Germany, France and the Netherlands have published detailed roadmaps to phase out oil, coal and gas, while around 130 countries, including the EU, opposed the text after the fossil fuel reference was dropped. UK climate envoy Rachel Kyte defended rejecting the deal, saying the process could be reshaped. The next summit, COP31, is due in about twelve months.

stories.headline: Stalking law simplified to become one offence
stories.claim: England and Wales will create a single standalone stalking offence, but the maximum sentence stays at 10 years.
stories.summary: England and Wales are to create a single standalone stalking offence, replacing the current two, after a review found the law "cluttered and confused". The government has accepted the change, which can be tried in either the Crown Court or magistrates' court. However, ministers rejected the reviewer's proposal to raise the maximum sentence from 10 to 14 years, arguing that the average sentence for the more serious offence was 18.6 months in the year to March. The review was led by Richard Wright KC, and the government has not yet committed to dropping the requirement to prove fear. Judge Loren AliKhan granted Disney and ABC a preliminary injunction and temporary restraining order, and refused the FCC's motion to dismiss the lawsuit. She wrote that the review was no coincidence, noting it began the day after Jimmy Kimmel joked about Melania Trump, and cited eleven occasions on which President Trump urged the FCC to strip ABC's licences. The FCC announced the review in April, even though most of the licences run until 2030 or 2031, and ordered the stations to submit renewals years early. The affected cities include New York, Los Angeles and Chicago. The judge declined to bar all formal or informal FCC pressure, saying ABC had not specified what those might be. The FCC, led by Brendan Carr, says the ruling is wrong and expects to prevail, arguing the review is part of a diversity-hiring inquiry.

stories.summary: US drinking water and industrial water systems are more exposed than official records suggest. The more pressing risk is access without exploits: 791 Rockwell MicroLogix 1400 controllers were internet-exposed as of 17 November, and most exposed Rockwell controllers sit on mobile networks via poorly secured cellular modems. stories.summary: The US Federal Communications Commission has given SpaceX conditional approval to deploy and operate a constellation of up to one million satellites for an orbital data centre business, a decision taken on Wednesday. The approval is a regulatory win for Elon Musk's plan to move AI computing into space, despite objections from Amazon, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society over debris, interference and environmental effects. The FCC set aside some of those concerns as outside its remit, and the order sets conditions on interference with US government systems in the 28.6-29.1 GHz band. It also deferred a decision on SpaceX's request to waive rules on satellite disposal, saying the company had not provided enough detail. SpaceX still needs further approvals, including a debris plan for satellites above 600 km, and has seven years to get its first satellite operational and 14 years to complete the constellation. Technical and funding hurdles, such as cooling chips in orbit and cutting launch costs, remain large, and critics note the economics are unproven.

stories.headline: Our ‘Paris manifesto’ proposes how to deal with extreme wealth in the AI age | Open letter
stories.claim: An open letter signed by economists and academics proposes a transnational coalition to curb extreme wealth and oligarchy in the AI age.
stories.summary: A broad group of economists, academics and writers, including Daron Acemoglu, Paul Krugman and Naomi Klein, has published a 'Paris manifesto' calling for a transnational coalition to curb extreme wealth. The letter notes that the wealth of about 3,000 households has grown from 3% of global GDP in 1987 to 17% now. It proposes a global tax floor of 2% of wealth for fortunes above $100 million, first floated in a G20 report in 2024 under Brazil's presidency, plus a one-time 'catch-up' levy. It also argues for limits on billionaire ownership of media and platforms, and for AI companies to consider non-profit foundation models. This is an opinion piece by signatories rather than a policy decision.
key_points: The open letter says the wealth of the richest 0.0001% rose from 3% of global GDP in 1987 to 17% today.

stories.headline: ‘It’s been really a mess’: Meta insiders concerned over push to AI content moderation
stories.claim: Meta employees say its shift to AI content moderation, amid mass layoffs, is causing mistakes and political concerns.
stories.summary: Meta employees say the company's push to replace human content moderators with AI is producing mistakes at a scale that could carry serious political consequences. Several staff describe moderation teams as skeleton crews, with some cut by half or two-thirds, and say they have found entire teams gone when they went to raise problems. The Guardian's sources say AI systems struggle with nuance, especially outside English, and often remove content that should stay up. Campaigners at Repro Uncensored counted 657 account takedowns on Meta platforms in the first half of 2026, up from 210 in all of 2025. Meta rejected claims of political bias, saying enforcement applies the same rules to everyone and that its newer AI systems catch violations more accurately.

stories.headline: Perplexity’s Time Machine lets AI agents search the web of the past
stories.claim: Perplexity launched Time Machine, letting AI agents search the web as it looked up to 365 days ago.
stories.summary: Perplexity has launched Time Machine, a tool that lets AI agents search and read the web as it stood on a chosen past date, going back up to 365 days. The aim is to stop AI models from peeking at later information when they are tested on forecasting, such as predicting elections. Perplexity says a model trained with the tool scored 0.80 on 2026 political events listed on Polymarket, just above the market's 0.79. The launch came a day after Epochal, a startup founded by three xAI co-founders, released a similar product with an archive of more than 30 years. Perplexity's own tests put leakage of later information at 0.25%, against 1.10% for rival Exa, though that check was run by Perplexity itself. The story also highlights a broader fight over web archives, with more than 241 news outlets now blocking the Wayback Machine.

stories.headline: China launches Shenzhou-24 carrying first foreign astronaut, a Pakistani, to Tiangong
stories.claim: China launched Shenzhou-24 on 25 November carrying Pakistani payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, the first foreign national to visit Tiangong.
stories.summary: China launched the Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on 25 November at 8.18am Beijing time, carrying Pakistani pilot Muhammad Zeeshan Ali to the Tiangong space station. Ali, 40, is the first foreign national to visit the station and the first Pakistani in orbit. He flies with Chinese commander Tang Hongbo and flight engineer Wu Yi aboard the spacecraft, which rode a Long March-2F rocket. Ali will serve as a payload specialist and stay for five to 10 days, running more than 90 experiments, including a photosynthetic cyanobacteria study, before returning on Shenzhou-23. He trained for seven months in Beijing, including Chinese-language study and calligraphy. The flight stems from a China-Pakistan space agreement signed in February 2025 and underlines Beijing's push to position Tiangong as an international cooperation hub as the ISS nears retirement around 2030. China aims for a crewed lunar landing by 2030, while NASA targets 2028 for its own Moon landing.

stories.headline: Shein to pay $100 million to settle US deceptive marketing claims
stories.claim: Shein agreed to pay $100 million to resolve US Federal Trade Commission allegations of deceptive marketing.
stories.summary: Shein has agreed to pay $100 million to resolve US Federal Trade Commission allegations that the fast-fashion retailer misled consumers about its products, suppliers and reviews. The FTC complaint, filed in a California federal court, says Shein screened consumer reviews illegally, gave inadequate customer service and misrepresented the country of origin and labour practices of its suppliers. Regulators allege that cotton described as US-grown was actually harvested in China. The settlement also sought an injunction against the practices. The privately held company has no public listing, so the payment affects it directly rather than a share price. The case highlights how US authorities are scrutinising origin and sourcing claims in consumer goods.

stories.headline: A year after Hong Kong's Wang Fuk Court fire, survivors mourn losses and seek accountability
stories.claim: Survivors of Hong Kong's Wang Fuk Court fire mark one year since the blaze that killed 168 people, still questioning accountability.
stories.summary: Survivors of the Wang Fuk Court estate in Tai Po are marking the first anniversary of the fire that killed 168 people, the deadliest blaze in Hong Kong since 1948, and many say they still feel no justice has been done. Many former residents plan to return to the estate on Thursday to mourn. The blaze tore through seven of the estate's eight 31-storey blocks, which had been wrapped in scaffolding and netting for renovation work. Last month, leader John Lee published an independent report that partly blamed four government departments and accepted the resignation of Housing Secretary Winnie Ho, the first official to step down over the fire. Lee also promised reforms, including laws to criminalise bid rigging in the renovation industry. The government has ruled out rebuilding on the original site and offered a buyback scheme, which most owners have accepted, but survivors such as Yip Ka Kui, whose wife died, say it does little to ease their sense of injustice. Authorities have ruled out commemorative events, though the Chief Secretary says lawful gatherings are permitted and destructive acts will be prosecuted.

stories.headline: Australia and Solomon Islands sign security treaty, a blow to China's Pacific influence
stories.claim: Australia and the Solomon Islands signed a sweeping security treaty in Canberra, naming Australia primary security partner and ruling out foreign bases.
stories.summary: Australia and the Solomon Islands signed a sweeping security treaty in Canberra on 25 November 2026, making Australia the island nation's "primary security partner" and ruling out any foreign military or security base on Solomon soil. Prime Minister Matthew Wale and 15 ministers attended the signing, which is widely seen as a counterweight to China's growing footprint in the Pacific. Australia will commit AU$740 million (about US$490 million) over ten years, including AU$670 million in grants and AU$70 million in concessional loans, for education, health, policing and climate resilience. The treaty bars militarisation or foreign interference in sensitive infrastructure such as airports, ports, energy and telecoms, but the clause is not retroactive, so existing Chinese-built assets are not covered. Wale is trying to unwind close ties with Beijing built under his predecessor Manasseh Sogavare, and said talks with China are ongoing; the 2022 China security pact is still being discussed and he cannot comment on it because of a non-disclosure clause. The opposition criticised the fast-tracking, and parliament returns in January to approve reforms.
key_points: Australia and the Solomon Islands signed a security treaty in Canberra on 25 November 2026, naming Australia the 'primary security partner'.
The treaty rules out any foreign military or security base on Solomon Islands soil.

stories.headline: China places Shanghai party chief Chen Jining under anti-graft investigation
stories.claim: China's anti-graft body has placed Shanghai Communist Party chief Chen Jining, a Politburo member, under investigation for suspected severe violations.
stories.summary: China's anti-corruption watchdog has placed Chen Jining, Shanghai's Communist Party chief and a member of the 24-strong Politburo, under investigation for suspected severe violations of discipline and law, a term that typically means corruption. The Central Commission for Discipline Inspection announced the probe on 24 November, and Xinhua gave no details of the alleged wrongdoing. Chen, 62, had been seen as a strong candidate for the Politburo Standing Committee, making his fall a significant setback. He is the fourth Politburo member investigated since 2025, after He Weidong, Zhang Youxia and Ma Xingrui, extending Xi Jinping's sweeping crackdown that has thinned China's senior leadership and military command. Shanghai's party paper pledged loyalty to Xi and said the anti-corruption campaign would not slow. Analysts say the probe deepens upheaval before the 2027 leadership reshuffle, and investors will watch for any effect on policy continuity in Shanghai, China's financial hub.

stories.headline: Kilmar Abrego Garcia leaves US for Spain, ending 20-month deportation fight
stories.claim: Kilmar Abrego Garcia has left the US for Spain on a commercial flight, ending a roughly 20-month deportation fight.
stories.summary: Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Salvadoran man wrongfully deported to El Salvador in March 2025, boarded a commercial flight from Washington Dulles to Madrid on Tuesday night, ending a long legal fight with the US government. The flight was delayed by several hours due to mechanical problems. According to the Washington Post, he agreed to leave under a deal with US authorities that would end removal proceedings, though Maryland court records had not yet reflected such an order. His lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said he chose Spain over a government flight to Liberia, and suggested he could return to the US later as the husband of a US citizen, possibly after Donald Trump's term ends. The White House and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin called the departure self-deportation and hailed it as a win. Senator Chris Van Hollen, who campaigned for his release, said Abrego Garcia left unharmed and with dignity as a free man. His case followed a sequence of events: he was held in the Cecot prison in El Salvador, returned to face human trafficking charges that were later dropped as politically motivated, and then faced attempts to send him to Uganda, Ghana and Liberia.

He reportedly agreed to leave under an arrangement that would end removal proceedings.
His lawyer said he avoided being sent on a government plane to Liberia and may return later as the husband of a US citizen.

stories.headline: Novartis CEO says AI will shave four years off drug development, not cure all disease
stories.claim: Novartis CEO says AI will cut drug development from 12 to eight years, far less than rivals' cure forecasts.
stories.summary: Novartis chief executive Vas Narasimhan has pushed back on claims that AI could cure cancer within five to 10 years, predicting a more modest effect on medicine. He expects AI to shorten average drug development from 12 years to eight within a decade and to lift clinical success rates from 8% to 12%. His view sits against Anthropic chief Dario Amodei, who suggested several major diseases could be cured within a decade, and Demis Hassabis, who said AI could defeat all diseases within 10 years. Narasimhan argues that limited understanding of human biology means lengthy animal and human trials will still be required. stories.headline: Britain bought fake C4 explosives for Ukraine

The product, EDC-4, was supplied by Tripwire South LLC, a firm founded by former Pennsylvania police sergeant Ryan Morris. UK Ministry of Defence tests after the first shipment found only PETN, which is more volatile, and an expert warned it is more prone to detonation from heat or friction. Tripwire said there was no safety risk and denied providing false information, while the MoD said the product was fit for purpose. The company's earlier explosives business had gone bankrupt in 2022, and Morris filed for personal bankruptcy in 2024 while already working with the British government.

Jurors acquitted the company of its most serious charge, racketeering conspiracy, and of conspiring to obstruct justice, a result Huawei's lawyer Brian Heberlig called a vindication. The case dates to 2018, when Meng Wanzhou, Huawei's chief financial officer, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, and to charges announced in 2019. Judge Ann Donnelly will sentence the company on 14 September 2027, with potential penalties running into billions of dollars. Huawei says it fully expects to appeal, and experts say the case has not hurt its business, which has grown in China's AI push.

stories.headline: Dutch court bars BYD Ti7 SUV from EU sales over Land Rover Defender design
stories.claim: A Dutch court banned sales of BYD's Ti7 SUV in the EU over a design-rights ruling in favour of Jaguar Land Rover; BYD plans to appeal.

BYD strongly disagrees, says the design is its own independent work and plans to appeal, and its shares were reported to have fallen. The ruling is a rare European test of copycat design claims against a Chinese carmaker.

stories.headline: Astronomers may have found a second Earth-like planet on the edge of our Solar System
stories.claim: A paper in MNRAS proposes a hidden 1.5–2 Earth-mass planet, dubbed PX2, at 200–500 AU to explain distant object orbits.
stories.summary: A new paper in the Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society suggests the Solar System may hide a second, smaller unseen planet, provisionally named Planet X2 or PX2. Led by Patryk Sofia Lykawa of the University of South Queensland and Kindai University, the modelling points to a body of roughly 1.5 to 2 Earth masses orbiting at 200 to 500 astronomical units. That is lighter and further out than the roughly ten-Earth-mass Planet Nine proposed by Caltech's Konstantin Batygin and Mike Brown about a decade ago. The model reproduces several odd orbits of distant icy bodies, such as the dwarf planet Sedna, though gaps with observations remain. The team suggests the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile could test the idea as it surveys the sky.
key_points: The paper was published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society on 23 November.
The proposed planet, PX2, has 1.5 to 2 times Earth's mass and orbits at about 200 to 500 AU.

stories.headline: 300,000 legal immigrants told they’re losing Medicare coverage
stories.claim: About 300,000 legal immigrants are told they will lose Medicare coverage under the new law, with cut-off set for 1 February.
stories.summary: The US Social Security Administration has told around 300,000 legal immigrants they may lose their Medicare coverage, a move that follows changes in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (H.R. 1). Recipients received letters warning coverage may end on 1 February unless they prove they remain eligible. Those affected include older and disabled non-citizens and people with end-stage renal disease, and immigrants who have paid more than $6 billion into the programme. Advocates say the law provides no exceptions and that some citizens could wrongly receive termination notices because of inaccurate records. The agency says it is administering the law passed by Congress and that people can appeal through a hotline or by uploading documents. From February 2027, only four categories of immigrants remain eligible, including refugees and asylum grantees.

stories.headline: Alberto Núñez Feijóo: One step away from running Spain
stories.claim: Alberto Núñez Feijóo's conservative PP is polling ahead of Pedro Sánchez's Socialists before Spain's 29 November election.
stories.summary: Spain's conservative opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo is the clear favourite to win the general election on 29 November, a vote that could make the 65-year-old the oldest man to become prime minister since the return to democracy. Polls show his People's Party slightly ahead of the Socialists under Pedro Sánchez, but he would probably need the far-right Vox to form a majority. Feijóo built his image as a pragmatic, unflashy manager during four consecutive terms as Galician regional president from 2009 to 2022. Critics point to controversies, including tactics in his first campaign and a tight grip on regional media, while the PP's own record has been clouded by corruption scandals in other parts of Spain. Spain is the European Union's fourth-biggest economy, and the result will shape its policy direction.

stories.headline: Ex-auxiliary police officer jailed after raising anti-terrorism barrier, causing bus crash at Changi Airport
stories.claim: A former auxiliary police officer was jailed eight weeks in Singapore for raising an anti-terror barrier that crashed a bus at Changi Airport.
stories.summary: A former Singapore auxiliary police officer was jailed for eight weeks on Wednesday after he negligently raised an anti-terrorism vehicle barrier as a public bus drove through Changi Airport Terminal 3. The incident happened in May 2024, when the bus hit the barrier and 22 people were taken to hospital, including the driver, who suffered a nasal fracture. Azfar Mustaqim Jasman, 26, pleaded guilty to causing grievous hurt through a negligent act, and was found to have leaned on the control panel in breach of standard procedure. The prosecution had sought seven to 10 weeks, while the defence asked for a fine. The barrier repair cost S$55,335 and the bus was written off at about S$236,516.

stories.headline: The rising cost of putting food on the table in India
stories.claim: India's food inflation rose to 8.94% in October, pushing headline retail inflation up to 6.09%.
stories.summary: Food prices in India are rising faster than the overall inflation rate, with food inflation hitting 8.94% in October. Headline retail inflation climbed to 6.09% from 5.54% in September, and rural food inflation reached 9.09%. Crisil's analysis found a home-cooked vegetarian thali cost 12% more than a year earlier, driven by onions, tomatoes, edible oil, rice and cooking gas. The monsoon was 13% below normal and El Niño conditions add risk, while the new CPI series gives food a smaller weight of 36.75%. The article highlights how food shocks can feed into broader wage-price pressures, a difficult balancing act for policymakers.

Food inflation surged to 8.94%, with rural areas at 9.09% and urban at 8.68%.

The southwest monsoon was 13% below normal, and intensifying El Niño adds risk to farm output.
Food now carries a 36.75% weight in the new consumer price index, down from 45.86% under the old series.
stories.market_take: Rising food inflation may keep the Reserve Bank of India cautious on rate cuts, a modest factor for Indian rupee and bond markets.

stories.headline: Have the US midterms brought an end to ‘nasty’ politics?
stories.claim: Analysis suggests US midterm campaigns saw attack ads and anti-trans messaging fall flat, with Democrats gaining from a more conciliatory tone.

Ohio's Amy Acton defeated Vivek Ramaswamy after his campaign aired a clip of her estranged mother calling her a liar, an ad a YouGov poll found 64 per cent of voters disapproved of once they knew the background. stories.headline: US Army to detonate about five tonnes of toxic lead azide in Iowa after court clears plan
stories.claim: US Army to detonate about five tonnes of lead azide at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant on Wednesday after appeals court clears the plan.
stories.summary: The US Army is set to detonate about five tonnes of degraded lead azide, a volatile compound, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday morning. The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals declined on Monday to block the operation, finding an emergency and adequate safeguards in place. The detonation has already been postponed three times, and President Trump had earlier paused it until courts and incoming Democratic governor Rob Sand agreed. Sand has not said whether he supports the move, while the current governor, Kim Reynolds, backs it. Environmental groups, including the Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club, warned of a plume of toxic lead particles and accused the government of bypassing the courts, arguing the EPA had not weighed the risks. The EPA issued an emergency permit covering 68 drums, citing an imminent threat to health and the environment. Officials say the material has degraded and that cold weather raises the risk of an uncontrolled explosion, which is why they consider it too unstable to store.

stories.headline: US blacklists Singapore-based Megaspeed and Alibaba-linked firms over Nvidia chip diversion
stories.claim: US Commerce Department blacklists Singapore-based Megaspeed and six other Southeast Asian firms over alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China.
stories.summary: The US Commerce Department has added Singapore-based Megaspeed International and six other Southeast Asian firms to its Entity List, a move that requires US licences for any future access to advanced American technology, including Nvidia's top AI GPUs. The listing, announced on Monday 23 November, came the same day Jensen Huang returned as Nvidia chief executive. The department said it suspected Megaspeed of routing Nvidia chips to Chinese companies in breach of export controls, after almost two years of investigation. Three of the listed firms are in Malaysia, one in Thailand and two in Singapore, and applications for licences are likely to be denied. Singapore's prime minister Lawrence Wong said his government is working with Washington on an enforcement mechanism, while noting Singapore lacks full information on chip end users. Malaysia's trade ministry will advise data centre operators not to host or serve the blacklisted firms, though this is advice rather than a ban. China has warned against a technological blockade.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO after Trump push; investigations and governance questions linger
stories.claim: Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO on 23 November after Trump pressed for his return; probes and congressional scrutiny continue.
stories.summary: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive, president and director with immediate effect on 23 November, less than two weeks after he resigned on 12 November. The board said US government input indicated his return poses no national security risk and that it was satisfied with his candour and ability to lead. Trump said he 'made the deal' by pressing the board, and VP JD Vance reportedly held a private call with Huang and reassured directors. Nvidia shares closed about 31% higher, adding nearly $1tn in market value, and the Nasdaq rose about 6.4%. Huang had stepped down after admitting an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based executive whom US intelligence has reportedly linked to a Chinese espionage network. Shares then fell 8.5% on Tuesday and remain about 37% below their October peak, and four congressional committees have asked Huang to testify while the SEC, Justice Department and an independent board probe continue. The episode matters because Nvidia is the world's most valuable chipmaker and its governance is now under political and legal scrutiny.
key_points: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, president and director with immediate effect on 23 November.
The board said US government input indicated his return poses no national security risk.
Nvidia shares closed about 31% higher on Monday, adding nearly $1tn in market value, and the Nasdaq rose about 6.4%.
Shares fell about 8.5% on Tuesday and were still down 37% from their early-October peak, according to later reports.
Huang faces questioning before four congressional committees, including a closed-door meeting with three House committees on 1 December, and he will speak at GTC Washington.
The SEC, Department of Justice and an independent board probe into security and IP leakage continue, and Senator Elizabeth Warren has demanded answers.
stories.market_take: Investors see Huang's return as a sign of continuity for Nvidia, which is a bellwether for the AI chip trade.

stories.headline: Amazon buys AI accelerator technology and staff from Israeli startup Decart
stories.claim: Amazon has agreed to acquire Decart's AI optimisation technology and its founders and engineers in a deal Bloomberg values at about $7.5bn; neither company has confirmed a price.
stories.summary: Amazon has agreed to acquire the proprietary AI optimisation technology of Israeli startup Decart, along with its three founders and engineering team, in a deal Bloomberg reports is valued at around $7.5 billion. The move follows earlier reports, from November, that Amazon was closing in on a deal of about $7.5bn including cash, stock and performance earnouts, with the Wall Street Journal first reporting talks around $7bn in October. Amazon describes the deal as an asset purchase rather than a whole-company takeover, so Decart's other models are not included and the startup's future is unclear. Neither company has disclosed a price. The Decart Optimization Stack sits between AI models and chips, tuning kernels, compilers and runtimes so accelerators stay fully utilised, and it supports Nvidia GPUs, Google TPUs and AWS Trainium chips. Amazon SVP Peter DeSantis framed the deal as a way to push Trainium and its AI efforts further. If the Bloomberg figure holds, it would rank among Amazon's largest acquisitions, behind its $8.5 billion purchase of MGM. The deal underlines Amazon's push to cut inference costs and make its own chips more competitive. Decart raised $300m in May 2026 at roughly a $4bn valuation.
key_points: Amazon has agreed to buy Decart's Optimization Stack technology and bring on its three founders and engineering team.
Bloomberg reports the deal is valued at around $7.5 billion; neither company has confirmed a price.
The deal is an asset purchase, so Decart's other technology is not included and its future is unclear.

Earlier reports had put talks at about $7bn, and Anthropic's roughly $6bn talks collapsed in September.
Decart raised $300m in May 2026 at roughly a $4bn valuation.
stories.market_take: A reported $7.5bn outlay is modest for Amazon's scale, but it signals a push to improve Trainium economics against Nvidia.

stories.headline: Japan opposition parties to submit motion to censure scandal-hit minister
stories.claim: Japan's opposition parties agreed to file a censure motion against education minister Yoshihiro Seki and to boycott a consumption tax cut bill.
stories.summary: Japan's opposition parties have agreed to submit a censure motion against education minister Yoshihiro Seki over a fundraising scandal, and to boycott deliberations on a key consumption tax cut bill. Senior officials from six opposition parties in the Senate reached the decision on Tuesday, with the motion possibly tabled this week. The scandal centres on revelations that senior bureaucrats gave presentations at Seki's fundraising parties, blurring official duties and political fundraising. Because the opposition holds a majority in the upper house, the censure motion could pass, though it would not be legally binding. The move threatens Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's plan to cut the consumption tax on food and drink for two years from April, as the current session ends on 12 December. Seki says he intends to stay on.

The opposition has agreed to boycott deliberations on the consumption tax cut bill for now.

stories.headline: Oil holds near three-month low as rising supply offsets Hormuz threat
stories.claim: Oil held near a three-month low on Tuesday as rising supply and expected surplus outweighed Hormuz shipping risks.
stories.summary: Oil prices hovered near a three-month low on Tuesday, with Brent at $88.97 a barrel, after posting their lowest close since 31 August on Monday. WTI was at $79.94, its lowest since late August. Rising supply, including Libya's restored Sharara pipeline flows, is weighing on prices, and Deutsche Bank estimates global observed inventories rose by 52 million barrels in October, implying a daily surplus of 1.7 million barrels. Risks persist, however: Iran's Revolutionary Guards said three tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, and US authorities are investigating possible Iranian involvement in cyberattacks on as many as 50 energy tankers. Analysts at ANZ say the market remains fragile with thin inventory buffers.

Libya's Sharara pipeline has reopened, adding supply.

stories.headline: COP31 talks in Antalya collapse over fossil fuel language; draft omits coal, oil and gas
stories.claim: COP31 talks in Antalya collapsed on Monday after more than two weeks of deadlock over fossil fuel and climate finance language.
stories.summary: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed on Monday after more than two weeks of contentious talks, making it the longest-ever UN climate negotiations, with countries unable to agree on fossil fuels or on money. Earlier, on the Sunday of overtime talks, the latest draft from the Turkish and Australian presidency again avoided naming coal, oil or gas, instead referring to the 2023 Dubai consensus on moving away from fossil fuels. About 130 countries, backed by the EU, wanted explicit transition language, while Saudi Arabia and other oil-rich states opposed it, and the EU raised the prospect of 'no deal'. Tuvalu's climate minister called the fossil fuel reference a red line. Other disputes included carbon capture and storage and a target for electricity to reach 35% of final energy by 2035. Developing nations objected to the removal of a US$120 billion climate adaptation target, and some delegates left, raising quorum concerns. Campaigners called it the 'worst COP ever', pointing to Berkeley Earth's finding that October 2026 was the warmest October on record. The breakdown undermines the idea of broad consensus on phasing out fossil fuels, a key goal of global climate diplomacy.
key_points: The longest-ever UN climate negotiations, COP31 in Antalya, collapsed on Monday without agreement on fossil fuels or climate finance.
The talks had been scheduled to end on Friday and ran into days of overtime.

stories.headline: BepiColombo spacecraft enter orbit around Mercury despite thruster glitch
stories.claim: BepiColombo entered orbit around Mercury, but a software glitch cut short a key thruster burn; ESA says the mission remains on track.
stories.summary: Europe's and Japan's joint BepiColombo mission has entered orbit around Mercury, becoming only the third spacecraft to visit the planet and the second to orbit it. The European Space Agency said on Monday that the mission remains on track and the spacecraft is in a stable orbit, despite a software glitch that cut short a key thruster burn. The 37-minute burn, begun about 635 km above the surface, was interrupted early, so the craft achieved roughly 77% of the planned velocity change, and it entered safe mode for a time. The spacecraft had travelled more than eight years and about 6bn miles to reach Mercury. Further thruster burns are scheduled in coming months to adjust the orbit. The two orbiters are still due to separate on 9 December, with one European and one Japanese craft. Routine science operations are expected to begin in April, and the orbiters should last about three years. The €1.6bn mission aims to explain how Mercury formed so close to the Sun, why it has a magnetic field, and what ice lies in its permanently shadowed craters.

The spacecraft entered safe mode for a time after the glitch.

stories.headline: Alice Huang chip-smuggling probe widens, drawing scrutiny of Nvidia and Lutnick
stories.claim: Scrutiny of Alice Huang's alleged chip network and Chinese intelligence ties has widened, with US senators and reports pressing Commerce and Treasury officials.
stories.summary: Scrutiny of Alice Huang, the Singapore-based former Megaspeed executive at the centre of the Nvidia affair, has widened as new reporting links her to Chinese intelligence and to alleged chip smuggling. The Financial Times and New York Times have tied her to a network that moved Nvidia chips into China, with the NYT citing a Strider Technologies analysis linking about $3.6bn of Chinese state money to her family's companies. Recent reports say US intelligence tracked her contacts with China's Ministry of State Security from spring 2025 until this autumn, and her business partner Kang Wei is also under federal examination. Senator John Kennedy has demanded that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent testify under oath, accusing the commerce department of incompetence or complicity. Nvidia says it has stopped H200 shipments to China, while Beijing calls the spy allegations a smear and Huang denies Chinese intelligence links. Her claimed career history has not been independently confirmed. The case is intensifying pressure on export enforcement and Nvidia's internal compliance culture.

stories.headline: Rajan Warns AI Boom Faces a Reckoning on Returns
stories.claim: Raghuram Rajan warns that AI infrastructure spending may not earn adequate returns, risking oversupply and valuation pressure.
stories.summary: Former Reserve Bank of India governor Raghuram Rajan has warned that the AI boom could face a reckoning over returns, arguing that the huge sums spent on computing capacity may never earn back their cost. He says supply could outrun demand because businesses are slow to adopt existing AI tools, and he points to OpenAI's output of 722 research manuscripts on 377 unsolved maths problems as an example of research that does not yet produce revenue. Rajan says AI model advantages last only one to two months and that debt-financed firms are most exposed. He made the case in a Bloomberg interview and in a 18 November essay. It is an opinion from a respected economist rather than new data, but it adds to investor debate about AI spending, and US political calls to pause data-centre approvals add to the friction.

stories.claim: Amazon is warning New Yorkers of up to $5 per order in fees as it campaigns against a city delivery bill backed by Mayor Mamdani.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani responded by accusing the company of greed, and Amazon has also put stickers on packages. The bill, introduced by Councilmember Tiffany Cabán, would require last-mile delivery firms, including Amazon and FedEx, to hire drivers as full-time employees and obtain city licences. Amazon says it might close its 15 city last-mile sites and cut about 2,000 jobs, and an Amazon-commissioned study estimates the extra cost at about $664 a year per New Yorker, or roughly $5.20 per package. Unions, Council Speaker Julie Menin and the mayor have accused the company of intimidation. The bill still has 35 co-sponsors, though one Queens councilman reportedly withdrew his support in September, and New York would be the first US city to adopt such rules.

stories.headline: Cisco and OpenAI launch Shirudo, open-source tool to defend against AI-driven attacks
stories.claim: Cisco and OpenAI have released Shirudo, an open-source eBPF tool that lets AI agents build temporary kernel-level shields for unpatched Linux systems.
stories.summary: Cisco and OpenAI have released Shirudo, an open-source tool that uses eBPF to apply temporary protections to Linux systems that cannot be patched quickly. The project was launched on 23 November 2026 as the number of software flaws surges, with more than 100,000 reported this year, many found by AI bug-hunting tools. Shirudo lets AI agents scan infrastructure and use OpenAI's Codex to write eBPF programs, called shields, that harden software without a patch or downtime. The companies say the approach has already mitigated recent Java flaws on an Elasticsearch deployment without interrupting service. Shields are meant to go live only once verified, and humans are expected to review each one before deployment. Cisco's Isovalent, which created Cilium and Tetragon, supplies the foundation for the tool, giving Cisco a commercial interest in wider eBPF adoption. Cisco's Jeetu Patel and OpenAI president Greg Brockman framed the project as a response to attackers who need only one unpatched machine.

The tool uses eBPF to insert protective programs into the Linux kernel without changing source code.

stories.headline: Paolo Bulgari, third-generation head of Bulgari jewellery dynasty, dies at 89
stories.claim: Paolo Bulgari, long-serving chairman of the Italian jewellery house Bulgari, has died in Rome aged 89.
stories.summary: Paolo Bulgari, a member of the family behind the Italian jewellery house Bulgari and a key figure in its growth into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged 89. His family announced the death on Saturday 21 November 2026, calling him the greatest jeweller of his time. He joined the family business in 1960 and became chairman in 1984, a post he held alongside his brother Nicola. Under the family, the house expanded into watches, which came to account for around 40 per cent of revenues, as well as perfumes and accessories, and he helped popularise coloured gemstones. Bulgari listed in Milan in 1995 and the family sold its controlling stake to LVMH in 2011 for about €3.7 billion, a move the family called painful but necessary. The family was acquitted of tax evasion charges in 2015, and in 2019 he founded the Paolo Bulgari Foundation with his wife to support education in disadvantaged parts of Rome.

stories.headline: Ascletis Announces Initiation of U.S. Phase I Study of ASC37i, a Potentially First-in-Class Once-Monthly to Once-Quarterly GLP-1R/GIPR/GCGR Triple Peptide Agonist, for the Treatment of Obesity – Company Announcement
stories.claim: Hong Kong-listed Ascletis has started a US Phase I trial of its once-monthly obesity drug ASC37i.
stories.summary: Ascletis Pharma, listed in Hong Kong under 1672, has begun a US Phase I trial of ASC37i, a once-monthly to once-quarterly obesity injection, after FDA clearance of its investigational new drug application. The triple peptide agonist targets the GLP-1, GIPR and GCGR receptors and is designed to be given by a thin-needle auto-injector. In mouse studies the company reports 88% greater relative weight loss than tirzepatide at the same dose, with up to 41.5% weight loss. In monkeys, the drug's half-life was about 17 days compared with 2.5 days for retatrutide. Because it is a biologic, it would face a longer exclusivity period under US rules. The data are preclinical and company-reported, and the trial is only at an early safety stage.
key_points: The US Phase I study of ASC37i has started after FDA clearance, in healthy adults with obesity or overweight.

Monkey studies show a half-life of about 17 days, roughly seven times longer than retatrutide.
As a biologic filed under a BLA, the drug would get 13 years of protection from price negotiations rather than nine.
stories.market_take: Positive read-across for the obesity-drug race, but early-stage data and a small Hong Kong listing mean limited near-term market effect.

stories.headline: Malaysia set to repatriate thousands more Myanmar migrants: PM
stories.claim: Malaysia will repatriate over 6,500 Myanmar migrants in December, including 1,500 by naval ship on 6-7 December.
stories.summary: Malaysia plans to send more than 6,500 Myanmar migrants back home in December, the largest announced round so far. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim told parliament on Tuesday that three naval ships will carry 1,500 Myanmar citizens on 6 and 7 December, while 5,303 more will be flown back during the month at Myanmar's expense. The move follows a September scheme that returned around 1,500 people, which rights groups say may endanger migrants by sending them back to a war-torn country. The announcement comes five days after the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, and that Myanmar must allow refugees to return safely. Kuala Lumpur had earlier said it would seek clarification after hundreds of returnees were reportedly held in military detention.

stories.headline: Can Burnham turn volume down on EU debate?
stories.claim: Burnham declined to rule out a future in/out EU referendum and set out a calmer approach to UK-EU ties after the summit.
stories.summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham has declined to rule out seeking a mandate for another EU referendum at the next general election, saying he would recommend one only if it served Britain's national interest. Speaking to the Commons after Friday's EU-UK summit in Brussels, he said there was 'no fixed destination' and promised no 'running commentary' on Europe. The government publishes its European Partnerships Bill on Thursday, with the legal text of the agreements due later in the week. Negotiations continue on university tuition fees for EU students, which both sides think is within reach within six months, and on the EU's common electricity market. Brussels is reportedly prepared to charge London for reinstating food export checkpoints if the UK reverses the food deal within ten years. The piece also notes the EU's willingness to include the UK in its 'Made in Europe' plan.

stories.headline: Coldest spell of autumn continues with risk of hill snow, ice and heavy rain

Hill snow, freezing rain and ice are possible on high ground such as the Grampians and the North Pennines, while milder, wetter air brings heavy rain to south-west England, Wales and Northern Ireland. The Met Office has issued a yellow warning for rain covering Cornwall and the Isles of Scilly from 10:00 GMT on Tuesday, with 30-40mm widely and up to 60-90mm possible in western Cornwall. Wednesday brings fog or freezing fog, mostly in Northern Ireland, before colder but mostly dry weather returns on Friday. Localised flooding and difficult driving conditions are possible.

stories.summary: Malaysia's Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim has told parliament that his government did not leak the minutes of the Pardons Board meeting on jailed former prime minister Najib Razak. He said neither the Legal Affairs Division nor the Attorney-General's Chambers circulated the document, and that the Home Ministry should investigate how it came to be published prematurely. Anwar argued that the Attorney-General had simply prepared a response to a court application, and that only the board's decision, not its minutes, had been requested. Lawmaker Ahmad Fadhli Shaari questioned whether the Official Secrets Act required declassification and why a third party had made the document public first. The row touches on Cabinet confidentiality and Najib's continuing legal battles.
key_points: Anwar told the Dewan Rakyat on Nov 24 that the government did not circulate the Pardons Board minutes on Najib Razak.

stories.headline: Moscow accuses Estonia of hostile actions on 'verge of triggering open war'
stories.claim: Russia's Foreign Ministry accused Estonia of hostile acts 'on the verge of triggering open war' after Tallinn announced a land border closure.
stories.summary: Russia's Foreign Ministry has accused Estonia of a range of hostile actions that are 'on the verge of triggering open war', escalating rhetoric after Tallinn announced it would close its land border crossings with Russia. Estonia plans to shut the crossings from December 1 for at least six months, after accusing Russian security services of staging an attempted arson attack on a defence company, which Moscow denies. Russia summoned Estonia's charge d'affaires in Moscow and accused Tallinn of letting Ukraine use its airspace, obstructing Russian cargo ships and banning Russian and Belarusian grain transit. Estonia denied allowing its territory to be used for Ukrainian military operations and its foreign minister accused Moscow of distracting from its own actions. The exchange deepens tensions on NATO's eastern flank.

stories.headline: Ebikes, screens and failing manners pose challenge for Dutch cycling culture
stories.claim: Dutch cycling culture faces strain from ebikes, screens and poor manners, prompting campaigns and a proposed helmet law.
stories.summary: The Netherlands, long the model of cycling, is struggling with a surge of ebikes, cargo bikes, fatbikes and scooters sharing its 23,000 miles of bike paths. Cyclist deaths rose by more than 50% between 2015 and 2025, according to the Netherlands Institute for Transport Policy Analysis. The Dutch government recently sent a bill to parliament proposing mandatory helmets for under-18s on ebikes, and Leiden has launched an awareness campaign under the slogan 'traffic is a team sport'. Officials and researchers warn that falling activity levels among young people are a public health concern, while others argue cars still cause most harm. The piece is a feature rather than a breaking development, but it highlights a wider policy debate over micromobility.

stories.headline: Fed's Williams says inflation still too high, signals more rate hikes possible

He hinted he favours a rate rise at the 8-9 December policy meeting and said he would not rule out raising rates at consecutive meetings if the economy proved strong. Markets broadly expect a quarter-point increase in December, taking the policy range from 3.75-4% higher, with further increases expected in 2027. Governor Christopher Waller has signalled he could back a larger half-point rise given hot price data. The comments came on the same day as a sharp stock rally sparked by Nvidia's leadership news, so the Fed signal sits alongside a strong equity market.

stories.headline: NATO calls urgent meeting as string of incidents escalates Russia tensions
stories.claim: NATO holds an urgent meeting after Russian missiles crashed in Poland, escalating tensions across Europe.
stories.summary: Nato's North Atlantic Council met urgently in Brussels on Monday after Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles crashed in southeastern Poland, with remnants found at three sites. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the airspace violation a deliberate provocation, though Nato's Mark Rutte said that had yet to be established. Warsaw has asked for more Nato forces and air-defence systems but has not invoked Article 4. German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said the incursions showed a pattern of Russian aggression, adding that Europe is 'not in war, but certainly not in peace'. The meeting comes amid a spate of incidents, including attacks on ships off Romania and an alleged Russian assassination plot in Denmark. The episode raises the risk of direct confrontation between Nato and Russia.

stories.headline: Russia’s war dead: the hidden toll of the Ukraine conflict
stories.claim: Analyses of leaked Rosstat records suggest Russian military deaths in Ukraine are far higher than officially acknowledged, at 490,000 or more.
stories.summary: Leaked Russian statistics agency records, analysed by several outlets, suggest the true toll of the war in Ukraine is far higher than officially acknowledged. One analysis puts Russian military deaths at 490,000 or more, while another estimate reported by The New York Times suggests over 700,000 Russian soldiers have died. The Financial Times reports that roughly one in every 17 deaths in Russia since 2022 may be linked to the war, and that Russian soldiers are twice as likely to die by suicide as civilians. The figures rest on leaked Rosstat data and independent analysis, so they are estimates rather than official counts. The findings matter because they challenge the Kremlin's published figures and shed light on the human cost of a conflict that has lasted since 2022.

stories.headline: Seino Holdings works with rivals for better, cleaner transportation
stories.claim: Japanese logistics firm Seino Holdings is partnering with rivals to share delivery networks and raise truck loading efficiency.
stories.summary: Japan's trucking sector has long run parallel delivery networks, with lorries from different companies often covering the same areas. Because shipments are small and return journeys are frequently empty, the loading efficiency of freight vehicles has stayed at roughly 40% of capacity for about 15 years. That waste pushes up costs and makes it harder to cut carbon emissions. Seino Holdings, a major Japanese logistics group, is working with rival firms to pool deliveries and fill more space on each trip. The feature is a reminder that cooperation between competitors may be one of the few practical ways to clean up freight transport in a sector under pressure from driver shortages and emissions targets.

stories.headline: Hobart's new $1.23 billion stadium price tag explained

stories.headline: DeepMind’s AI agents found cheaper quantum algorithms, and proved them
stories.claim: Google DeepMind agent teams found much cheaper quantum algorithms for fusion, chemistry and drug design, with results proved in Lean.
stories.summary: Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI say teams of Gemini 4 agents have found quantum algorithms that are far cheaper to run for fusion, chemistry and drug-design problems, and proved each result correct in the Lean theorem prover. The biggest gain is a laser-driven fusion fuel calculation that becomes 11.8 times cheaper, with error-corrected qubit needs falling from 5,650 to 4,338. A simulation of a light-sensitive molecule is about eight times cheaper, the cost of simulating Cytochrome P450, an enzyme that breaks down most medicines, falls 2.5 times, and a widely used maths routine becomes more than 290 times cheaper. The circuits are too large to test on today's machines, which is why formal proofs were used, and an outside checker re-ran every proof to rule out gaming. DeepMind cautions the workloads will still need far more resources than the first error-corrected quantum computers will offer, and has open-sourced its Lean library and results.

It arrives after enterprise pushback over the 30-day data retention Anthropic introduced when it launched Fable 5. Under EFS, prompts and replies sit in the customer's own Amazon or Google cloud account, encrypted so that not even the customer can read them, and nobody at Anthropic or the cloud provider sees them. More than 100 customers helped build it, including Bridgewater, Salesforce and Stripe, and Wells Fargo has publicly backed the approach. The system is free, though customers pay their cloud provider for storage, and it follows OpenAI's similar Private Safety Processing preview in August.

stories.claim: Amazon's Leo satellite internet is falling behind SpaceX's Starlink after launch partner setbacks grounded its rockets.

Amazon's last successful Leo deployment was 12 weeks ago, on 2 July, aboard a ULA Atlas V rocket. Its main alternatives are grounded: ULA's Vulcan has been out since February after a booster anomaly, and Blue Origin's New Glenn has been down since its only launchpad was destroyed in May. Amazon has also ordered more Ariane 6 launches, but a component issue is expected to disrupt them for the rest of 2026. The FCC has extended Amazon's deadline to launch half of its planned 3,232 satellites, on condition that it moves quickly. SpaceX is meanwhile preparing to launch its first Starlink V3 satellites on Starship.

stories.headline: Estudio A-G uses colour to update 1960s book-lined house in Mexico City
stories.claim: Estudio A-G has renovated Casa Magnolia, a 1962 Mexico City house, using bold colour and a sculptural timber structure.
stories.summary: Mexico City studio Estudio A-G has renovated Casa Magnolia, a 1962 house in San Ángel designed by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio as a library for his brother. The 275-square-metre interior was completed in February 2026 and uses colour as the main architectural tool, with soft blue walls, plum sofas and moss-green chairs. A dark timber structure rises through split levels like a sculptural tree, and original bookshelves and flooring were restored. The studio also replaced windows and glass, updated services and rebuilt the kitchen and bathrooms. The project shows how a mid-century house can be made contemporary without nostalgia.
key_points: Casa Magnolia was built in 1962 by Jaime Ortiz Monasterio as a library for his book-collecting brother.
Estudio A-G, led by Andrés Gutiérrez, was commissioned in 2025 and completed the work in February 2026.
A dark timber structure rises through split levels to a double-height ceiling as the central spatial anchor.
Colour blocks, including soft blue walls, plum sofas and terracotta marble, organise the space.
Original bookshelves and wood flooring were restored, and custom furniture was designed to sit with historic pieces.

stories.headline: At least 31 killed as fuel tanker crash ignites large fire on Cairo highway
stories.claim: A fuel tanker crash on a Cairo highway has killed at least 31 people and set off a large fire.
stories.summary: A fuel tanker crashed on a Cairo highway and ignited a large blaze, killing at least 31 people according to the Guardian's report. The feed gave no further detail on the cause, the number of vehicles involved or the injured. Road accidents involving fuel tankers are a recurring and deadly problem in Egypt, where poor enforcement and ageing vehicles often raise the death toll. The story is a significant local tragedy with international reach given the death toll, though it carries no direct market relevance.
key_points: A fuel tanker crash on a Cairo highway caused a large fire.
At least 31 people have been killed, according to The Guardian.
The feed summary gives no details on cause or the injured.
Egypt has a history of deadly road accidents involving fuel tankers.

stories.headline: Marjorie Taylor Greene lambasts Trump and Hegseth over ‘dirty bomb in Iowa’
stories.claim: Marjorie Taylor Greene condemns the US Army's planned detonation of lead azide in Iowa, calling it a dirty bomb risk.
stories.summary: Former Republican congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene has attacked the Trump administration and Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over a US Army plan to detonate five tons of lead azide at an ammunition facility in Middletown, Iowa. She called for them to be locked up and described the blast as a potential Chernobyl-scale event. The Army said the detonation was controlled and mitigated, and FEMA advised residents to relocate or stay indoors. Environmental groups have filed lawsuits to halt the blast. The story is a domestic political and environmental dispute, scheduled around the Thanksgiving holiday.
key_points: Greene, who broke with Trump last year, accused Trump and Hegseth of planning to detonate a 'dirty bomb' in Iowa.
The US Army plans to detonate five tons of lead azide at Middletown, Iowa, scheduled for Wednesday morning.
Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said the blast would be controlled and preferable to an uncontrolled detonation.
FEMA advised Middletown residents to relocate, and the Army warned vulnerable groups to avoid outdoor activity.
Environmental groups filed lawsuits last week seeking to halt the explosion.

stories.headline: Netanyahu says corruption trial ‘must end’ as court suggests dropping case
stories.claim: Netanyahu demands an end to his corruption trial after judges signal dropping or reconsidering several cases.
stories.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, still in a caretaker role, has called for his long-running corruption trial to end after judges cast doubt on the charges and recommended dropping or reconsidering several cases. In Case 4000, the most serious bribery case, judges indicated little chance of conviction. The Attorney General said she would consider the recommendations. The developments come as Netanyahu fights for political survival after inconclusive elections on 27 October, with opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot now tasked with forming a government by 6 December. Parliament also gave preliminary approval to a probe into the 7 October attack and a bill that would bar indicted prime ministers from serving.

Netanyahu called the cases 'fabricated' and said the trial must end immediately.
